docs.title: amesml
docs.text:
Reproducible Ames Housing price prediction as an installable package, a command-line tool and a REST API.

amesml turns a university house-price notebook into software you can install, test, version and deploy. It predicts the sale price of a house in Ames, Iowa from 79 property features, and separately whether it sells at or above the median price.

pip install amesml
amesml train --model gbm

docs.title: Why amesml
docs.text:
• Reproducible. The default models reproduce the original notebook's published results to the cent, every model is seeded, and each saved model records the exact configuration, library versions and a fingerprint of the data it was trained on.
  • Installable. A typed Python package with a CLI, tested on Linux, macOS and Windows across Python 3.9-3.13, with 99% test coverage.
  • Serveable. A FastAPI service with validated requests and an OpenAPI page, packaged as a Docker image that starts with trained models.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Decisions made while turning the coursework notebook into the amesml package, with the evidence behind each. Entries marked Deviation differ from the original specification for the conversion; each says why.

docs.title: D1. The defaults reproduce the notebook exactly
docs.text:
The package's first promise is reproducibility, so TrainConfig() with no arguments rebuilds the notebook's models: the same 80/20 split with seed 42, the same column typing, imputation and encoding, LinearRegression for price and LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000) for the class. Every improvement (engineered features, regularised models, gradient boosting) is opt-in.

Result, verified by tests/test_notebook_parity.py on the real data: MAE $21,139.99, RMSE $31,790.77, R² 0.8682386; accuracy 0.9452, precision 0.9254, recall 0.9538, F1 0.9394, confusion matrix [[152, 10], [6, 124]] - identical to the notebook's recorded outputs.

docs.title: D2. The notebook's linear regression was solved by LSQR, and amesml keeps it so
docs.text:
The first version of the package produced dense design matrices and got MAE $20,893 and R² 0.853 - not the notebook's numbers, although logistic regression matched exactly. The cause: scikit-learn's ColumnTransformer returns a sparse matrix when fewer than 30% of entries are non-zero, which is true here (34 numeric columns beside about 250 one-hot columns). For sparse input LinearRegression does not solve least squares exactly; it runs the iterative LSQR solver, which stops at a tolerance on this ill-conditioned, unscaled, rank-deficient design. The notebook's published figures are LSQR's solution. (Logistic regression converges to the same optimum either way.)

amesml keeps scikit-learn's default sparse output for the linear models, so the defaults reproduce the notebook, and gives a dense matrix only to gradient boosting, which rejects sparse input. The exact least-squares solution is slightly worse on R² (0.853), so nothing is lost.

docs.title: D3. Feature engineering is optional and off by default
docs.text: Deviation. The specification asked for feature engineering "reproduced from the notebook", but the notebook engineers no features. features.py implements the standard Ames derivations (total square footage, house age, remodel age, total bathrooms, porch area) as pure functions, enabled with engineer_features: true. Turning them on by default would have broken D1. Cross-validation shows they help gradient boosting (CV RMSE $29,586 to $28,881) and make little difference to the linear models, whose features they nearly duplicate. The remodel age is clipped at zero because one record lists a remodel after its sale year.

docs.title: D4. Only NA and empty fields mean "missing"
docs.text: In this dataset NA encodes absence ("no pool"), while the string "None" is a real category (MasVnrType). pandas' default missing-value list includes "None", so read_ames_csv uses keep_default_na=False with NA and "" only - as the notebook did. Adding "" changes nothing for the Kaggle file (it has no empty fields) and makes user-supplied CSVs more forgiving.

docs.title: D5. Missing categories become an explicit "Missing" level
docs.text:
Deviation. The specification suggested most-frequent imputation for categorical columns. In Ames a missing PoolQC means "no pool"; filling it with the most frequent value among houses that do have a pool would invent a pool. amesml fills text columns with the constant "Missing", as the notebook did. Category codes stored as numbers (MSSubClass, MoSold) get their own branch with most-frequent imputation, because one column cannot be encoded when it mixes the string "Missing" with integers.

None and pd.NA are converted to NaN before imputation: under pandas 2 an object column keeps Python None, which SimpleImputer does not treat as missing and which would otherwise become a category of its own. Found by the Python 3.9/3.10 test runs.

docs.title: D6. drop_first stays on, and unseen categories are reported by name
docs.text: The notebook one-hot encoded with drop="first", avoiding the dummy-variable trap for the unregularised models, and dropping it changes the results. With drop set, scikit-learn warns on every call that meets a category absent from training, naming columns only by position ("columns [14, 29]"). amesml silences that warning and reports the values itself - {"RoofMatl": ["Membran"], "Electrical": ["Mix"]} on the reference split - in Predictions.unseen_categories, the CLI log and the API response.

docs.title: D7. What ridge and lasso mean for classification
docs.text:
ridge is L2-penalised logistic regression and lasso is L1-penalised logistic regression - the standard "ridge/lasso logistic regression" - with C = 1 / alpha, so in both tasks a larger alpha means a simpler model. RidgeClassifier was rejected because it has no predict_proba, and the API returns probabilities. L1 uses the liblinear solver: same scores as saga, in 0.4 s instead of 14 s.

scikit-learn 1.8 deprecated LogisticRegression(penalty=...) (removal in 1.10) in favour of l1_ratio, but before 1.8 l1_ratio is ignored unless penalty="elasticnet". l1_logistic_regression chooses the right spelling for the installed version; both branches are tested.

docs.title: D8. Default regularisation strengths come from cross-validation on the training split
docs.text: alpha defaults are 10 (ridge) and 300 (lasso) for regression, 30 and 3 for classification. Each was chosen by 5-fold cross-validation on the 1,168 training rows with the final preprocessing. The test rows were never used: picking defaults by test score would leak the test set into the model. One early experiment illustrates why this matters: a log-transformed target looked better on the test split (R² 0.913) but was far worse under cross-validation (RMSE $40,428 against $33,170), because of a few extreme houses.

docs.title: D9. Scale only where it matters
docs.text: Numeric features are standardised for the penalised and logistic models, which need it. Plain least squares is scale-invariant and the notebook did not scale it (scaling would also change the LSQR path in D2); tree models split on thresholds and ignore scale.

docs.title: D10. The classification threshold comes from the training rows
docs.text: threshold: median resolves to the median sale price of the training rows ($165,000 on the reference split), as in the notebook, so no test price influences the model. With stratify: true the split is balanced on the full-data median, which only shapes the split; the model's threshold is still re-derived from its training rows.

docs.title: D11. The dataset download is pinned to a commit and checksummed
docs.text: Deviation. The specification suggested the Kaggle mirror or the De Cock original from jse.amstat.org. Kaggle requires a login, and the De Cock file has 2,930 rows with different column names (a separate adapter, listed on the roadmap). download_ames fetches this repository's own data/train.csv at a fixed commit - an immutable URL - checks its SHA-256 before writing anything, and writes through a temporary file so a failed or tampered download never replaces good data. An explicit missing path is never downloaded to; only the default location is.

docs.title: D12. .gitattributes keeps the dataset byte-identical on every platform
docs.text: The original clone of this repository on Windows produced train.csv with CRLF line endings (Git for Windows defaults to core.autocrlf=true), whose hash no longer matched the pinned checksum. GitHub's Windows runners use the same default. data/** -text stops Git from rewriting the data on any platform.

docs.title: D13. A model is a directory with a checksum
docs.text: save_model writes model.joblib beside metadata.json (configuration, metrics, input features and defaults, the training data's fingerprint, library versions and the model file's SHA-256), and train adds metrics.json. load_model refuses a model file whose checksum no longer matches. This catches corrupted and swapped files; it is not a security boundary, because unpickling executes code. The documentation says to load only trusted models.

docs.title: D14. Training-data fingerprints are platform-independent
docs.text: dataset_fingerprint hashes the frame serialised as CSV with \n line endings, not the source file, so the same data has the same fingerprint on every operating system and regardless of the file it came from. amesml evaluate uses it to warn when you score a model on its own training data.

docs.title: D15. Omitted fields take training defaults; null means absent
docs.text: A request that leaves a field out gets the model's typical training value. That value counts "missing" as a value of its own: for PoolQC the most common value is missing (no pool). Ignoring missing values would make the default "Gd" and give every house with an unspecified pool a good one. A field sent as null means "absent" and is handled exactly as in training.

docs.title: D16. Unknown request fields are rejected
docs.text: {"GrLivAre": 1500} returns 422 Unknown feature(s): GrLivAre instead of silently pricing a house of default size. Text in a numeric field is also a 422. One process can serve one model per task; AMESML_MODEL_PATH takes a comma-separated list.

docs.title: D17. Models load at startup, and startup fails loudly
docs.text: A missing or invalid model stops the service before it accepts requests, so a misconfigured container fails its deployment instead of its first user.

docs.title: D18. Python 3.9 stays supported, and is proven by tests, not by mypy
docs.text:
Python 3.9 reached end of life in October 2025, but the specification asked for it, and supporting it costs little. mypy 2 can no longer target 3.9, so python_version = "3.10" in the mypy configuration and 3.9 compatibility is established by running the full suite on 3.9 (locally and in CI). The test matrix is Linux, macOS and Windows × Python 3.9, 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13; the whole suite was also run locally on 3.10. Python 3.10 and 3.13 are added to the classifiers because they are tested.

The declared minimum versions (pandas>=1.5, numpy>=1.23, scikit-learn>=1.3, typer>=0.9, fastapi>=0.100, and so on) were verified by resolving the lowest allowed versions on Python 3.9: all 224 tests pass, apart from two warnings raised inside those old libraries (Starlette 0.27's test client leaves a stream open; joblib 1.3 cannot count CPU cores on Windows 11, which removed wmic).

docs.title: D19. Runtime-annotated modules spell unions with Optional
docs.text: Typer reads the CLI's signatures, and Pydantic the API's models, at runtime. Python 3.9 cannot evaluate X | None at runtime, so cli.py and api.py use Optional[...] and skip from __future__ import annotations. Every other module uses the modern syntax. A comment in each file explains why.

docs.title: D20. matplotlib is an optional plots extra
docs.text: Deviation. The core dependency list has no plotting library, and the API image should not carry one, so plotting is the plots extra rather than a core dependency. plots.py uses matplotlib's object-oriented Figure API and never touches pyplot, so it keeps no global state and needs no display.

docs.title: D21. A test extra, and pinned linters
docs.text: Deviation. The specification listed test tools under dev. A smaller test extra installs on every supported Python and is what the CI matrix uses. dev adds the tooling, which needs Python 3.11+ (pre-commit and pandas-stubs); environment markers keep pip install -e ".[dev]" working on older versions. ruff and mypy are pinned exactly so CI cannot start failing without a code change; Dependabot proposes upgrades.

docs.title: D22. Tests treat every warning as an error
docs.text: filterwarnings = ["error"] makes deprecations fail the build while they are still cheap to fix. Two third-party warnings are ignored, each with a comment: Starlette's notice when its test client falls back from httpx2 (which needs Python 3.11+) to httpx, and pyparsing deprecations triggered inside the old matplotlib that Python 3.9 receives. The test extra installs httpx2 where it can.

docs.title: D23. Licence metadata uses the PEP 639 expression only
docs.text: Deviation. The specification listed a "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT" classifier. With license = "MIT" (a PEP 639 licence expression), PEP 639 forbids licence classifiers alongside it, and PyPI enforces this at upload - a rejection that twine check does not catch, so it would surface only during a release. The expression alone conveys the licence.

docs.title: D24. The README uses absolute image URLs
docs.text: The README is also the PyPI project description, where relative image paths break. Images point at raw.githubusercontent.com so they render on both.

docs.title: D25. The Docker image serves gradient boosting and trains it if needed
docs.text: The benchmark shows gradient boosting is the strongest model for both tasks, so the image serves regression-gbm and classification-gbm. If the build context contains trained models they are copied; otherwise the builder stage trains them from data/train.csv, so docker compose up works from a fresh clone. .dockerignore is an allowlist (only the package, data and models are sent), the runtime stage holds just the virtual environment and the models, and the service runs as a non-root user with a health check.

docs.title: D26. Release and docs workflows guard themselves
docs.text: The release workflow refuses a tag that does not match the package version, publishes with PyPI trusted publishing (no stored token), then creates the GitHub release with generated notes using the gh CLI rather than a third-party action. The docs workflow also builds on pull requests, so a broken page is caught before merge; it deploys only from main. CI smoke-tests the built wheel and the running Docker container over HTTP.

docs.title: D27. Notebooks, the report and the old models are preserved
docs.text: Nothing was deleted. The notebook keeps its place with outputs stripped (so diffs stay readable), and the untouched original with every output is in notebooks/archive/. The PDF report moved to docs/. The notebook's pickled models moved to models/notebook/ with a note: they record no library version and are superseded by amesml train. requirements.txt remains as a pointer to .[notebook], so old instructions still work. Ruff excludes notebooks/.

docs.title: D28. Documentation stays on MkDocs Material for now
docs.text: The specification asked for MkDocs Material. Its maintainers have announced end of life on 5 May 2027, with Zensical as the successor and a compatibility path for existing mkdocs.yml files. Material is fully supported until then, so the site uses it as specified; migrating before May 2027 is a small, mechanical follow-up.

docs.title: Bugs found by testing across environments
docs.text:
Running the suite on five Python versions and the minimum dependencies found real defects before any user did:

  • Lost log lines. The CLI's log handler did not flush, so under Click 8.1 (Python 3.9) warnings from commands that then succeeded were silently lost.
  • None as a category under pandas 2 (D5).
  • Read-only arrays. Under pandas 3 copy-on-write, np.asarray on a frame returns a read-only view; the missing-value normaliser now copies.
  • Mangled install hint. Rich parsed [api] in pip install "amesml[api]" as markup and printed pip install "amesml". All interpolated CLI output is now escaped.
  • Click 8.2 removed CliRunner(mix_stderr=...) while Python 3.9 can only install Click 8.1, which needs it; the tests handle both.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    raw[(train.csv)] --> data["data<br/>load, validate,<br/>split, fingerprint"]
    data --> features["features<br/>engineered columns<br/>(optional)"]
    features --> preprocess["preprocess<br/>impute, encode, scale"]
    preprocess --> model["models<br/>linear / ridge /<br/>lasso / gbm"]
    model --> evaluate["evaluate<br/>metrics"]
    model --> bundle[("model bundle<br/>model.joblib<br/>metadata.json")]
    bundle --> cli["cli<br/>amesml predict"]
    bundle --> api["api<br/>FastAPI service"]
    config["config<br/>TrainConfig"] -.-> model

The features, preprocess and estimator steps form a single scikit-learn Pipeline, so a saved model applies exactly the same transformations to new data as it learned in training. Everything statistical (medians, category levels, scaling, the classification threshold) is fitted on the training rows only.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Module Responsibility config TrainConfig: every training option, validated, loadable from YAML or JSON data Ames schema, CSV conventions, validation, checksummed download, splitting, fingerprints features Pure functions deriving total area, ages, bathrooms and porch area preprocess Column typing and the ColumnTransformer (imputation, one-hot encoding, scaling) models Estimators, training, the model bundle on disk, input alignment and prediction evaluate Regression and classification metrics as typed dataclasses plots Figures, drawn with matplotlib's object-oriented API cli The amesml command (Typer) api The REST service (FastAPI) errors The exception hierarchy

Dependencies point one way: cli and api use models, which uses preprocess, features, data and evaluate. Only cli writes to the terminal; library code logs through logging.getLogger("amesml").

docs.title: The preprocessing transformer
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    input[raw columns] --> num["numeric<br/>median imputation (+ scaling)"]
    input --> zero["numeric_zero_fill<br/>MasVnrArea, GarageYrBlt -> 0 (+ scaling)"]
    input --> cat["categorical<br/>missing -> 'Missing', one-hot"]
    input --> codes["categorical_codes<br/>MSSubClass, MoSold: mode, one-hot"]
    num & zero & cat & codes --> matrix[design matrix]

Scaling is applied only where it matters (the penalised and logistic models). The matrix is sparse for the linear models - scikit-learn's default, and the reason the defaults reproduce the notebook exactly - and dense for gradient boosting, which requires it.

docs.title: A saved model
docs.text:
models/regression-gbm/
├── model.joblib     fitted pipeline, with task_, input_features_, feature_defaults_, ...
├── metadata.json    config, metrics, features, defaults, data fingerprint,
│                    library versions, SHA-256 of model.joblib
└── metrics.json     held-out metrics

load_model refuses a model.joblib whose checksum no longer matches its metadata. The API reads metadata.json for /model/info.

docs.title: Serving
docs.text: create_app() loads every model once at startup, keyed by task, and fails to start if any is missing or invalid, so a misconfigured container crashes immediately instead of failing on its first request. Requests are validated by Pydantic, aligned to the model's columns by records_to_frame, and scored by the same predict function the CLI uses.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text: Every push runs ruff, the ruff formatter, strict mypy, the test suite with coverage on Linux, macOS and Windows for Python 3.9, 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13, a distribution build with twine check, a Docker build with an HTTP smoke test, a strict documentation build, and CodeQL.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Every model family on the Kaggle Ames training data (1,460 sales), with each model's default configuration. Two views of each model:

  • Held-out test: the notebook's split (80/20, seed 42; 292 test houses). The linear rows reproduce the published notebook results exactly.
  • 5-fold CV: cross-validation over all 1,460 houses, mean ± standard deviation. Less dependent on which houses land in one split, so this is the column to compare models by.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
• alpha is the regularisation strength; for classification C = 1 / alpha. Defaults were chosen by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split only (see Design decisions).
  • On a single split, small differences are noise: the CV standard deviations show how much a score moves between folds.
  • Engineered features (total area, ages, bathrooms, porch area) help gradient boosting. For the linear models they are almost exact linear combinations of existing columns, so they change little.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and the project uses Semantic Versioning.
First packaged release of the house-price-prediction coursework as amesml.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• amesml Python package with a typed public API: load_ames, build_preprocessor, train_regressor, train_classifier, train, evaluate_regressor, evaluate_classifier, predict, save_model and load_model.
  • Defaults that reproduce the original notebook's published results exactly (linear regression MAE $21,139.99, R² 0.868; logistic regression accuracy 94.5%, F1 93.9%).
  • Ridge, lasso and histogram gradient-boosting models for both regression and above/below-median classification, with cross-validated default regularisation.
  • Optional engineered features: total area, house and remodel age, total bathrooms and porch area.
  • TrainConfig, loadable from YAML or JSON, with validation of every option.
  • Dataset loading with schema validation and a checksummed, atomic download pinned to an immutable URL.
  • Model bundles with metadata.json: configuration, metrics, feature defaults, training-data fingerprint, library versions and a checksum of the model file.
  • amesml command-line interface: data download, train, evaluate (including --split test to reproduce held-out metrics), predict, plots and serve.
  • FastAPI service with /predict, /predict/class, /health and /model/info, partial-record support and reporting of unseen categories.
  • Multi-stage Docker image and Docker Compose file.
  • Figures drawn with matplotlib: price distribution, missing values, residuals, confusion matrix and permutation importance.
  • Test suite with 99% coverage, run on Linux, macOS and Windows for Python 3.9-3.13.
  • CI, release (PyPI trusted publishing), documentation, CodeQL, labeler and stale-issue workflows, plus Dependabot.
  • MkDocs Material documentation: user guide, model card, benchmarks, architecture, design decisions and API reference.
  • Contributing guide, Code of Conduct, security policy, governance, support page, citation metadata, and issue and pull request templates.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Repository reorganised: the report moved to docs/, the notebook's pickled models to models/notebook/, and the notebook is committed with its outputs stripped (the original is kept in notebooks/archive/).
  • The author name and the licence's copyright holder corrected to Muhammad Ahsan.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for helping improve amesml. Bug reports, documentation fixes and new features are all welcome. By taking part you agree to follow the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
The package supports Python 3.9+; the development tools need Python 3.11 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/Ahsan-muhd-444/house-price-prediction.git
cd house-price-prediction
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
make install                       # pip install -e ".[dev,docs]" and pre-commit hooks

Without make (for example on Windows), run the commands from the Makefile directly.

docs.title: Make targets
docs.text: Target Runs make lint ruff check . and ruff format --check . make format applies ruff's fixes and formatting make typecheck mypy src (strict) make test pytest with coverage; fails below 85% make build builds the sdist and wheel, then twine check make docs mkdocs build --strict; make docs-serve previews it make docker builds the API image make benchmark re-runs scripts/benchmark.py and rewrites docs/benchmarks.md make clean removes build output and caches

docs.title: Tests and checks
docs.text:
Before opening a pull request, run:

make lint typecheck test docs
  • Tests use a synthetic Ames-shaped dataset from tests/conftest.py, so they need no download. tests/test_notebook_parity.py also checks the published results against the real data/train.csv.
  • Warnings are errors in the test suite. If a dependency starts warning, fix the cause; add a filter to pyproject.toml only for third-party noise, with a comment saying why.
  • New behaviour needs tests. Coverage is above 99%; please keep it there.
  • Library code logs through logging.getLogger("amesml") and never prints.

docs.title: Branches and pull requests
docs.text:
1. Open an issue first for anything larger than a small fix, so the approach can be agreed before you write code.
  2. Branch from main: feat/short-description, fix/... or docs/....
  3. Keep each pull request to one change, with tests and documentation.
  4. Fill in the pull request template. CI must pass before review.
  5. The maintainer squash-merges; the pull request title becomes the commit message, so it must follow the convention below.

docs.title: Commit messages
docs.text:
Conventional Commits:

feat: add an XGBoost model option
fix: keep "None" as a MasVnrType category when reading CSVs
docs: explain partial records in the REST API guide
test: cover the 503 path for a missing classifier
ci: cache pip downloads in the docs workflow
chore: bump ruff to 0.18

Use feat!: or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer for incompatible changes.

docs.title: Releasing (maintainers)
docs.text:
1. Update CHANGELOG.md: move items from Unreleased under a new version heading with the date.
  2. Bump __version__ in src/amesml/_version.py (semantic versioning).
  3. Commit (chore: release vX.Y.Z), then tag and push:
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "amesml vX.Y.Z"
git push origin main vX.Y.Z
  1. The release workflow checks that the tag matches the version, builds the distributions, publishes them to PyPI with trusted publishing and creates a GitHub release with generated notes.

docs.title: Model card
docs.text: Following the structure of Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting (FAT* 2019). It covers the models amesml trains with its defaults; the numbers come from scripts/benchmark.py and the held-out split described below.

docs.title: Model details
docs.text:
• Developer: Muhammad Ahsan, Software Engineering, COMSATS University Lahore.
  • Version: amesml 0.1.0 (November 2026).
  • Type: supervised tabular models built with scikit-learn.
    • Regression predicts the sale price in US dollars.
    • Classification predicts whether a house sells at or above a threshold price - by default the median sale price of the training rows ($165,000 on the reference split).
  • Families: ordinary least squares / logistic regression (the original notebook's models), ridge and lasso (L2- and L1-penalised), and histogram gradient boosting.
  • Inputs: up to 79 property attributes from the Ames dataset (size, quality and condition ratings, age, location, amenities, sale type).
  • Licence: MIT.
  • Contact: GitHub issues.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
• Primary use: teaching, learning and demonstrating a reproducible, production-style machine-learning workflow: packaging, testing, serving and documenting a model end to end.
  • Primary users: students, instructors and engineers studying ML engineering practice.
  • Out of scope: pricing, buying, selling, lending, insuring, taxing or appraising real property. The models describe one Iowa city between 2006 and 2010; they do not know today's market, other regions, or anything not in the 79 columns. Do not use them for decisions that affect people.

docs.title: Factors
docs.text: The data contains no information about buyers, sellers or occupants. Relevant factors are properties of the houses: price band, age, neighbourhood, size and quality. Neighbourhood is a feature, and because neighbourhood composition can correlate with protected characteristics, location-driven predictions can encode historic patterns of segregation and lending (see Ethical considerations).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• Regression: mean absolute error (dollars; easy to interpret), root mean squared error (penalises large misses), R² and mean absolute percentage error (comparable across price levels).
  • Classification: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC. The classes are balanced by construction (the threshold is a median), so accuracy is meaningful; ROC-AUC measures ranking independent of the threshold.
  • Uncertainty: a single 292-house test split is noisy, so models are also compared with 5-fold cross-validation (mean ± standard deviation).

docs.title: Training and evaluation data
docs.text:
• Dataset: the Kaggle House Prices: Advanced Regression Techniques training file - 1,460 residential sales in Ames, Iowa, 2006-2010, with 81 columns (an Id, 79 candidate features and SalePrice). It is a subset of the 2,930-sale dataset compiled by De Cock (2011) from the Ames City Assessor's Office.
  • Preprocessing: NA means "absent" (no pool, no basement) and becomes an explicit Missing category; numeric gaps take the training median, except veneer area and garage year where a gap means "none" and becomes 0. Category codes (MSSubClass, MoSold) are one-hot encoded. All statistics are learned from the training rows only.
  • Split: 80% training (1,168 houses), 20% held out (292), shuffled with seed 42 - the notebook's split.

Price band Houses Linear MAE Linear MAPE Boosting MAE Boosting MAPE under $130k 83 $16,703 19.4% $12,089 15.0% $130k-165k 81 $18,284 12.6% $10,479 7.2% $165k-215k 60 $16,846 9.0% $11,867 6.3% over $215k 68 $33,747 10.0% $34,544 10.6% House age at sale Houses Linear MAPE Boosting MAPE 0-10 years 83 9.2% 7.8% 11-40 years 91 11.9% 8.6% over 40 years 118 17.0% 12.6%

Relative error is highest for the cheapest and oldest houses - roughly twice the error rate of mid-market houses. Absolute error is highest for the most expensive houses, and the largest single misses are luxury homes that both models under-predict by around $200,000 (a $755,000 sale predicted at about $504,000 by gradient boosting).

docs.title: Ethical considerations
docs.text:
• Uneven accuracy falls on cheaper homes. If these models were used to value property, owners of lower-priced and older homes would see the least accurate estimates relative to their home's value - the same groups for whom an error matters most. This is the main reason the intended use excludes real decisions.
  • Location as a proxy. Neighbourhood strongly drives predictions. In housing, location-based valuation has historically carried discriminatory lending and appraisal patterns; a model trained on past sales reproduces past prices, including any bias in them.
  • No personal data. The dataset describes properties and sales, not people.

docs.title: Caveats and recommendations
docs.text:
• The data is from 2006-2010, one city, and includes the start of the 2008 housing crash. Prices since then are not represented.
  • Four sales have more than 4,000 sq ft of living area. Two are priced like ordinary houses ($160,000 and $184,750) and are true outliers; De Cock recommends removing houses over 4,000 sq ft for teaching use. The models keep them, as the notebook did.
  • A handful of categories occur only in the test split (for example the Membran roof material); unseen categories are reported, not silently guessed.
  • Prefer the cross-validated scores when comparing models; the single split's differences are often within noise.
  • Retrain and re-evaluate before any use outside this dataset.

docs.title: amesml.config
docs.text:
Training configuration.

A :class:TrainConfig records every choice that changes a trained model. It is saved inside each model's metadata.json, so any model can be retrained exactly from its own metadata.

The defaults reproduce the original notebook: an unregularised linear model (or a logistic regression for classification) on the raw Ames columns, with an 80/20 split seeded with 42.

docs.title: TrainConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Everything that determines how a model is trained.

Attributes:

Name Type Description task TaskType

"regression" predicts the sale price; "classification" predicts whether a house sells at or above threshold.

model ModelType

Estimator family. linear is ordinary least squares (or logistic regression for classification), ridge and lasso add L2 and L1 penalties, gbm is histogram gradient boosting.

target str

Name of the sale-price column.

id_column str | None

Identifier column that is never used as a feature.

test_size float

Fraction of rows held out for evaluation.

random_state int

Seed for the train/test split and every seeded estimator.

Use exactly these numeric columns instead of inferring them from the data.

categorical_features tuple[str, ...] | None

Columns stored as numbers that are really category codes, such as the dwelling-type code MSSubClass.

Numeric columns where a missing value means "none of this", so they are filled with 0 instead of the median.

Drop the first level of each one-hot encoded column, as the notebook did. This avoids the dummy-variable trap for the unregularised models.

docs.title: amesml.data
docs.text:
Loading, validating and splitting the Ames Housing dataset.

The dataset is the Kaggle "House Prices: Advanced Regression Techniques" train.csv: 1,460 sales from Ames, Iowa, with 79 candidate features, an Id and the target SalePrice (De Cock, 2011).

In this file the string "NA" is a value, not an accident: it means the house has no pool, no alley access, no basement, and so on. Elsewhere the literal word "None" is a real category (MasVnrType == "None"), so pandas' default list of missing-value markers - which includes "None" - would silently destroy information. :func:read_ames_csv therefore treats only "NA" and empty fields as missing, exactly as the original notebook did.

docs.title: amesml.preprocess
docs.text:
Column typing and the scikit-learn preprocessing transformer.

The transformer reproduces the notebook's choices, which follow from what a missing value means in this dataset:

  • Numeric gaps are filled with the training median - except columns listed in zero_fill_cols (MasVnrArea, GarageYrBlt), where a gap means the feature is absent rather than unknown.
  • Categorical gaps become the explicit level "Missing". NA in Ames means "no pool", "no basement" and so on; filling it with the most frequent level would claim that houses without a pool have the most common pool quality.
  • Category codes stored as numbers (MSSubClass, MoSold) get their own branch, filled with the most frequent code, because a column cannot mix the string "Missing" with integers and still be encoded.

docs.title: amesml.models
docs.text:
Training, saving, loading and prediction.

A trained model is an ordinary scikit-learn Pipeline with a few extra fitted attributes that make it self-describing:

task_ "regression" or "classification". input_features_ The raw columns the pipeline expects, in order. input_kinds_ "number" or "text" for each input column, used to coerce inputs. feature_defaults_ The most common training value of each input (the median for numeric measurements), used for any column an input leaves out. threshold_ Classification only: the price separating the two classes. training_data_sha256_ Fingerprint of the rows the pipeline was fitted on. amesml_config_ The :class:~amesml.config.TrainConfig used, as a dictionary.

On disk a model is a directory holding model.joblib and metadata.json (and metrics.json when it came from :func:train).

docs.title: amesml.api
docs.text:
REST inference service.

Install with pip install "amesml[api]" and start it with amesml serve, or run uvicorn amesml.api:app with AMESML_MODEL_PATH set.

Models are loaded once, when the application starts. AMESML_MODEL_PATH (or create_app(model_paths=...)) may list one regression and one classification model, separated by commas, so a single process can serve both endpoints.

Pydantic and FastAPI evaluate annotations at runtime, and Python 3.9 cannot evaluate X | None; this module therefore spells unions with Optional and Union and does not use from __future__ import annotations.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Every command has --help. Global options go before the command: amesml -v train ... shows debug logging, amesml -q train ... only warnings.

Command Does amesml data download Download data/train.csv and verify its checksum amesml train Train a model, print held-out metrics, save it amesml evaluate Score a saved model on labelled data amesml predict Predict for every row of a CSV amesml plots Regenerate the figures from the data amesml serve Run the REST API

Errors are reported on one line with exit code 1; usage errors exit with 2.

docs.title: train
docs.text:
amesml train                                   # the notebook's linear regression
amesml train --model gbm                       # gradient boosting
amesml train --task classification             # the notebook's logistic regression
amesml train --config examples/config.example.yaml --name my-model

The model is saved to models/<task>-<model>/ (change with --out and --name) as three files:

  • model.joblib - the fitted scikit-learn pipeline
  • metadata.json - configuration, metrics, feature defaults, library versions, a fingerprint of the training data and a checksum of model.joblib
  • metrics.json - the held-out metrics alone

--task and --model override the configuration file.

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
amesml evaluate --model models/regression-gbm --data data/train.csv --split test

--split test recreates the exact rows the model was held out on, so it reproduces the metrics printed at training time. --split train scores the training rows, and --split all (the default) every row; amesml warns when those include rows the model was fitted on.

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
amesml predict --model models/regression-gbm --input houses.csv > predictions.csv
amesml predict --model models/classification-gbm --input houses.csv --out classes.csv

The input uses the Ames column names; NA and empty cells mean missing. Columns the model does not use (such as SalePrice) are ignored, columns it needs but the file lacks are filled with typical training values, and an Id column is copied to the output. Regression writes predicted_price; classification writes predicted_label (1 = at or above the threshold) and probability_above_threshold.

docs.title: plots
docs.text:
pip install "amesml[plots]"
amesml plots --out images/

Writes the sale-price distribution, missing values per column, residuals of the linear model, the classifier's confusion matrix and the gradient-boosting model's permutation importance, as images/amesml_*.png.

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
amesml serve --model models/regression-gbm --model models/classification-gbm

Serves at most one model per task. Without --model, the comma-separated paths in AMESML_MODEL_PATH are used. --host and --port also read AMESML_HOST and AMESML_PORT. See REST API.

docs.title: data download
docs.text:
amesml data download                      # to data/train.csv
amesml data download --out elsewhere/     # to elsewhere/train.csv
amesml data download --url URL --sha256 HASH

The default source is pinned to a commit of this repository and checked against a SHA-256 before anything is written.

docs.title: Configuration file
docs.text:
Training options live in a TrainConfig, which can be written as YAML or JSON and passed with amesml train --config FILE or TrainConfig.from_file(FILE). Unknown keys are rejected, so a typo cannot silently fall back to a default.

# Every TrainConfig option, with its default. Use with:
#   amesml train --config examples/config.example.yaml
# Command-line --task and --model override the values here.

task: regression            # regression | classification
model: gbm                  # linear | ridge | lasso | gbm
target: SalePrice
id_column: Id
test_size: 0.2
random_state: 42

# Classification only: a price, or "median" for the training rows' median.
threshold: median
stratify: false             # classification only

# Derived features: total area, house and remodel age, bathrooms, porch area.
engineer_features: true

# Leave unset to infer column types from the data.
numeric_features: null
categorical_features: null
categorical_codes: [MSSubClass, MoSold]
zero_fill_features: [GarageYrBlt, MasVnrArea]

drop_first: true
alpha: null                 # ridge/lasso strength; null = cross-validated default
max_iter: 5000

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning task regression regression predicts the price; classification predicts at/above threshold model linear linear, ridge, lasso or gbm (see below) target SalePrice target column id_column Id identifier, never used as a feature test_size 0.2 share of rows held out by train random_state 42 seed for the split and every seeded estimator threshold median classification: a price, or the training rows' median stratify false classification: keep the class balance in both splits engineer_features false add total area, ages, bathrooms and porch area numeric_features inferred use exactly these numeric columns categorical_features inferred use exactly these categorical columns categorical_codes [MSSubClass, MoSold] numeric columns that are category codes zero_fill_features [GarageYrBlt, MasVnrArea] numeric columns where missing means "none" drop_first true drop one level per one-hot encoded column alpha per model regularisation strength for ridge and lasso max_iter 5000 iteration limit for iterative solvers

The defaults reproduce the original notebook exactly.

docs.title: Model families
docs.text:
model Regression Classification Default alpha linear ordinary least squares logistic regression (C = 1) - ridge ridge regression L2-penalised logistic regression 10 / 30 lasso lasso L1-penalised logistic regression 300 / 3 gbm histogram gradient boosting histogram gradient boosting -

For classification C = 1 / alpha, so in both tasks a larger alpha means a simpler model. The defaults were chosen by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split; see Design decisions.

docs.title: Overriding feature types
docs.text:
Setting numeric_features or categorical_features replaces the inferred list for that role only; the other role is still inferred from the remaining columns. To train on a handful of columns, set both:

numeric_features: [GrLivArea, OverallQual, YearBuilt, TotalBsmtSF, GarageCars]
categorical_features: [Neighborhood]

With engineer_features: true the engineered columns are added to the numeric features, and the raw columns they need are read even if not listed.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The image serves the REST API with a gradient-boosting regressor and classifier.

docker compose up --build
# or
docker build -t amesml .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 amesml

Then open http://localhost:8000/docs.

docs.title: How the image is built
docs.text:
• Two stages. The builder installs amesml[api] into a virtual environment and prepares the models; the runtime stage copies only the environment and the two model directories onto a clean python:3.11-slim.
  • Models. If models/regression-gbm and models/classification-gbm exist in the build context they are used as they are. Otherwise they are trained from data/train.csv during the build, so the image always starts with working models.
  • Small context. .dockerignore is an allowlist: only pyproject.toml, README.md, LICENSE, src/, data/ and models/ are sent to the build.
  • Non-root. The service runs as an unprivileged amesml user.
  • Health check. Docker polls GET /health.

docs.title: Serving other models
docs.text:
Mount a model directory and point AMESML_MODEL_PATH at it:

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$(pwd)/models/regression-linear:/models/regression-linear:ro" \
  -e AMESML_MODEL_PATH=/models/regression-linear \
  amesml

Note

A model trained outside the container may have been pickled with a different scikit-learn version. scikit-learn warns about this when loading; the safest course is to train inside the same image.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: Everything the CLI does is available from Python. The main entry points are importable from the top-level package.

docs.title: Train and evaluate in one call
docs.text:
from amesml import TrainConfig, load_ames, train

houses = load_ames()  # data/train.csv, downloaded if missing
result = train(houses, TrainConfig(model="gbm"))

result.metrics  # RegressionMetrics(mae=16826.0, ...)
result.metrics.to_dict()
result.save("models/regression-gbm")

train splits the rows with test_size and random_state, fits on the training rows and scores the rest. The returned TrainResult also carries train_rows, test_rows, dataset_sha256 and any unseen_categories found in the test rows.

docs.title: Control the split yourself
docs.text:
from amesml import TrainConfig, evaluate_classifier, predict, train_classifier
from amesml.data import train_test_split_df

train_df, test_df = train_test_split_df(houses, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
model = train_classifier(train_df, TrainConfig(model="lasso"))

predictions = predict(model, test_df)
labels = (test_df["SalePrice"] >= model.threshold_).astype(int)
evaluate_classifier(labels, predictions.values, predictions.probabilities)

train_regressor and train_classifier fit on every row they are given and return a scikit-learn Pipeline. It works with scikit-learn tooling directly (model.predict(frame)), and carries a few extra fitted attributes:

Attribute Meaning task_ "regression" or "classification" input_features_ raw columns the model reads feature_defaults_ typical training value per column threshold_ classification only: the price separating the classes training_data_sha256_ fingerprint of the training rows

docs.title: Predicting
docs.text:
amesml.predict(model, frame) is the safest way to score new data: it aligns and type-checks the columns, fills missing ones, and reports categories the model never saw:

result = predict(model, new_houses)
result.values  # prices, or labels for a classifier
result.probabilities  # classifier only
result.unseen_categories  # e.g. {"Neighborhood": ["Atlantis"]}
result.to_frame()

docs.title: Save and load
docs.text:
from amesml import load_metadata, load_model, save_model

save_model(model, "models/my-model")
model = load_model("models/my-model")  # verifies the file's checksum
metadata = load_metadata("models/my-model")

Warning

Models are pickled. Loading one runs code, so only load models you trust. The checksum detects corrupted or swapped files; it is not a security boundary.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
from amesml import add_engineered_features, build_preprocessor, infer_feature_types

types = infer_feature_types(houses)  # numeric vs categorical columns
transformer = build_preprocessor(types.numeric, types.categorical, scale=True)
houses_plus = add_engineered_features(houses)  # TotalSF, HouseAge, ...

See the API reference for every function.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Every error amesml raises on purpose derives from amesml.AmesMLError: AmesSchemaError (bad columns or values), ConfigError, DatasetDownloadError and ModelLoadError. Each also derives from the closest built-in (ValueError or RuntimeError).

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
pip install "amesml[api]"
amesml serve --model models/regression-gbm --model models/classification-gbm

The service loads its models once at startup and refuses to start if a model is missing or invalid. Interactive documentation is served at /docs, and the OpenAPI schema at /openapi.json.

docs.text: Method Path Returns GET /health status, version and which tasks have a model GET /model/info the metadata.json of each loaded model, by task POST /predict predicted sale prices POST /predict/class price class and probability for each house

docs.title: Predicting
docs.text:
Send up to 1,000 houses as records:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @examples/predict_request.json

{
  "predictions": [180571.47, 145403.74],
  "model": {
    "task": "regression",
    "model": "gbm",
    "estimator": "HistGradientBoostingRegressor",
    "amesml_version": "0.1.0",
    "created_at": "2026-11-01T11:10:18+00:00"

{
  "predictions": [
    {"label": 1, "above_threshold": true, "probability": 0.9431},
    {"label": 0, "above_threshold": false, "probability": 0.0003}
  ],
  "threshold": 165000.0,
  "model": {"task": "classification", "model": "gbm"},
  "warnings": []
}

docs.title: Partial records
docs.text:
Records use the Ames column names. You do not have to send all 79:

  • Leave a field out and it takes the model's typical training value: the median for measurements, the most common value for everything else.
  • Send null to say the feature is absent - for example "PoolQC": null for a house without a pool. This is how the dataset encodes absence, and the model handles it exactly as it did in training.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Status When 422 an unknown field name (so typos fail loudly), text in a numeric field, an empty or oversized batch 503 no model is loaded for the requested task

Categories the model never saw in training (an unknown Neighborhood, say) do not fail the request. They are listed in warnings and encoded as the column's reference category.

docs.text:
Variable Default Meaning AMESML_MODEL_PATH - comma-separated model paths, one per task AMESML_HOST 127.0.0.1 interface to bind AMESML_PORT 8000 port
